newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Bells poised for stock recovery as Q1 nears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Bells poised for stock recovery as Q1 nears.

text.p: The uncertainty which has clouded investment demand for U.S. telephone firms is starting to clear, and if investors do return, regional Bells rather than long distance companies look poised to benefit.
Share analysts say first quarter earnings starting next week will show strong profits to back the impression that the Bells are riding high and due for a stock price recovery.
"Stock prices appear to more than discount competitive and regulatory dangers," said Bette Massick of Bear Stearns, who this week urged investors to go overweight in regional Bells.
Analysts believe it is now clearer that the regulatory changes will be manageable for the Bells, and competition will probably not bite this year. Yields are attractive too.
"We believe the real battle for market share will be 1998 and beyond," said Linda Meltzer of UBS Securities.
Telephone stocks peaked in February last year, when the Telecom Act paving the way for full competition in the industry became law, but have underperformed the market since.
For example, local phone companies underperformed the S&P 500 by 25 percent in 1996, despite strong profit growth.
The Bells are Ameritech Corp, BellSouth Corp and U S West Inc, plus SBC Communications Inc, which just bought Pacific Telesis Group, and merger partners Bell Atlantic Corp and NYNEX Corp.

The picture for long distance companies is more cloudy. AT&T Corp already signalled its first quarter results will be lower while MCI Communications Corp and Sprint Corp are weighed by dilution from new ventures.
"The long distance companies will have more difficulty," said Robert Wilkes of brokers Brown Brothers Harriman.
Operating results will reflect the buoyant marketplace, but heavy spending will restrict net earnings, say analysts.

AT&T told analysts in March that first quarter earnings would be as much as 10 percent below the $0.76 per share earned in 1996's first quarter, as it invests to prepare for new wireless and local telephone markets.

MCI is in the process of merging with British Telecommunications Plc, which has supported its share price, and is drawing back from the melee in the fierce long distance market, which will slow revenue and volume growth.
"By MCI's standards it will be an unusually weak quarter for volume growth in part because of their concentration on high margin customers," said Meltzer.
Sprint is weighed by its ambitious wireless venture and big spending at Global One, its international venture with France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom AG .

The Bells are still notching up impressive growth from extra phone lines bought for access to the Internet and for facsimile machines, and are pretty much ready for long distance service inside their own territories.
Nevertheless there are still plenty of pitfalls to avoid.
"They have to control their expenses for the new markets that are opening up," said Simon Flannery of J.P. Morgan.
Rising interest rate may lower their yield appeal too.
Investors may still be cautious because of Federal Communications Commission decisions due on access charges and universal service.
"The Bell stocks are awaiting regulatory rulings due in the second quarter, and are certainly a lot cheaper than a year ago," said Wilkes.
The big three long distance firms are entering the local calling market cautiously. AT&T has begun in California while MCI is concentrating on local calling for businesses.
Local phone company GTE Corp, which is not a Bell and has already begun offering long distance services, is expected to perform strongly in the first quarter.
"Their growth will be at the high end of the group and their cellular growth will be very strong," Meltzer said.
